set1.q: Which test is the gold standard for vasospastic angina?
opts: Provoked spasm at angiography
Correct. The gold standard is coronary artery spasm during angiography when ergonovine or acetylcholine is delivered, then resolved with nitroglycerin given through the catheter.
Exercise treadmill test
Vasospasm occurs at rest, so an exertional test does not reproduce it. The gold standard is spasm provoked at angiography with ergonovine or acetylcholine.
Nuclear stress test
A nuclear stress test separates reversible from fixed perfusion defects in atherosclerotic disease. The gold standard for vasospasm is spasm provoked at angiography.
Coronary calcium score
A calcium score is for risk stratification, not for acute disease or spasm. The gold standard for vasospastic angina is provoked spasm at coronary angiography.

set1.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
set1.q: Which item is scored in the HEART score?
opts: Ejection fraction
Ejection fraction needs an echocardiogram and is not a HEART component. The score uses history, electrocardiogram, age, risk factors and troponin.
Heart rate
Heart rate is not scored. HEART (History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, Troponin) uses those five items only.
Age
Correct. The HEART (History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, Troponin) score rates history, the electrocardiogram, age, risk factors such as diabetes and smoking, and the initial troponin.
Blood pressure
Blood pressure is not scored on its own; hypertension enters only as one of the risk factors. The five components are history, electrocardiogram, age, risk factors, troponin.

set1.q: What is the first-line drug therapy for vasospastic angina?
opts: Calcium channel blockers
Correct. First-line therapy for vasospastic angina is a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem or amlodipine, with smoking cessation and nitrates for symptoms.
Nonselective beta blockers
Nonselective beta blockers are on the avoid list for vasospastic angina, with aspirin and triptans. First-line therapy is a calcium channel blocker.
Daily aspirin
Aspirin is to be avoided in vasospastic angina, although it is standard in atherosclerotic disease. First-line therapy is a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem.
Triptans
Triptans can precipitate vasospasm and are to be avoided. First-line therapy for vasospastic angina is a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem or amlodipine.

set1.q: The sinoatrial node branch arises from the right coronary artery in about what share of people?
opts: About 10%
Ten percent badly understates it. The right coronary artery supplies the sinoatrial node in about 60% of people, the circumflex in about 40%.
About 60%

Correct. The right coronary artery supplies the sinoatrial node in about 60% of people and the left coronary artery, through the circumflex, in about 40%, so a bradyarrhythmia cannot pin the culprit for certain.
About 40%
About 40% is the circumflex share: in those people the left coronary artery supplies the sinoatrial node. The right coronary artery supplies it in about 60%.
About 95%
Nearly everyone is the atrioventricular node, which the right coronary artery supplies. The sinoatrial node comes from the right coronary artery in about 60% only.

set1.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
set1.q: After infarction, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are especially indicated for which patients?
opts: Reduced left ventricular function

Correct. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors reduce myocardial remodeling (scarring) and are indicated with reduced left ventricular function to prevent dilation and heart failure; most patients go home on one.
Vasospastic angina

Vasospastic angina is treated first-line with calcium channel blockers, plus smoking cessation. The post-infarction indication for an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is reduced left ventricular function.
Right ventricular infarct

The defining rule in a right ventricular infarct is to withhold nitroglycerin because the ventricle is preload dependent. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors target reduced left ventricular function.
Bradycardia after infarction
Bradycardia is the reason to hold a beta blocker in acute infarction. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are indicated for reduced left ventricular function, to prevent dilation.

set1.q: What does plain old balloon angioplasty leave out that percutaneous coronary intervention includes?
opts: A balloon
The balloon is the whole of plain old balloon angioplasty: it dilates the narrowed vessel. What the procedure leaves out is the stent that percutaneous coronary intervention places.
A guidewire
Both procedures begin with catheterization, the introduction of a guidewire into the heart and coronary arteries. The difference is the stent, which only the intervention leaves behind.
Contrast dye
Both procedures rely on angiography, dye that identifies the lesion. What balloon angioplasty alone leaves out is the stent that keeps the artery open after the balloon is removed.
A stent
Correct. Plain old balloon angioplasty opens a narrowed artery without using a stent. Percutaneous coronary intervention places a drug-eluting or non-drug-eluting stent to keep the artery open.

set1.q: Which is a proposed mechanism of microvascular angina?
opts: Complete heart block
Complete heart block is a conduction problem tied to the right coronary artery's supply of the atrioventricular node. Endothelial dysfunction is a proposed microvascular mechanism.
Endothelial dysfunction

Correct. Proposed mechanisms of microvascular angina include endothelial dysfunction, myocardial ischemia, insulin resistance or diabetes, abnormal autonomic control, altered cardiac sensitivity, estrogen deficiency and altered pain perception.
Plaque rupture
Plaque rupture with platelet activation and thrombus drives the acute coronary syndromes. Endothelial dysfunction is a proposed mechanism of microvascular angina.
Aortic valve narrowing
Aortic valve narrowing is a valvular cause of angina, not a microvascular mechanism. Endothelial dysfunction and estrogen deficiency are proposed mechanisms.

set1.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
set1.q: Why can nitroglycerin cause shock in a right ventricular infarct?
opts: Lost preload drops output
Correct. The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent; decreasing preload reduces the Frank-Starling effect, the ventricle fails into right-sided heart failure, output falls and shock follows.
It triggers major bleeding
Bleeding is the danger of thrombolytics, not nitroglycerin. Nitroglycerin causes shock here by lowering the preload the right ventricle depends on.
It provokes coronary spasm
Nitroglycerin relieves coronary spasm rather than causing it. The problem in a right ventricular infarct is the fall in preload and output.
It blocks the atrioventricular node
Nitroglycerin does not block conduction. In a right ventricular infarct it drops the preload the failing right ventricle needs, and output falls.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following coronary artery disease:
set1.q: Which is a modifiable coronary risk factor?
opts: Male sex
Sex is nonmodifiable: men carry more risk than premenopausal women. A sedentary lifestyle is modifiable.
Age over 55
Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor (men from 45, women from 55). A sedentary lifestyle can be changed.
Family history
Early infarction or sudden death in a first-degree relative is a genetic, nonmodifiable factor. A sedentary lifestyle is modifiable.
Sedentary lifestyle
Correct. Modifiable risk factors are obesity, dyslipidemia, diabetes, smoking, hypertension, excessive alcohol, sedentary lifestyle and ineffective management of stress.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following coronary artery disease:
set1.q: At its core, what is myocardial ischemia?
opts: An oxygen supply and demand mismatch
Correct. Ischemic heart disease is fundamentally a mismatch between the oxygen the myocardium demands and the oxygen its coronary supply delivers: the heart writes checks its vasculature cannot cash.
A failure of electrical conduction
Conduction failure, such as heart block, can follow ischemia, but it is a consequence. Ischemia itself is a mismatch between myocardial oxygen demand and oxygen supply.
Inflammation of the pericardial sac
Pericardial inflammation is pericarditis, which can follow an infarction as a complication. Ischemia is a mismatch between myocardial oxygen demand and supply.
A primary defect of one heart valve
A valve defect is valvular heart disease. Ischemia is defined by the balance of oxygen: myocardial demand outstrips what the coronary circulation supplies.

set1.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following coronary artery disease:
set1.q: What is a coronary calcium score used for?
opts: Finding the culprit artery today
The culprit artery is found at coronary angiography. The calcium score stratifies long-term risk and plays no role in an acute event.
Measuring the ejection fraction
Ejection fraction comes from an echocardiogram. A calcium score stratifies long-term coronary risk, higher scores meaning higher risk.
Long-term risk stratification
Correct. A cardiac computed tomography calcium score (0 to 400 or more, higher meaning higher risk) stratifies future risk. It is not a test for acute coronary syndrome.
Diagnosing acute coronary syndrome
The calcium score is specifically not for acute coronary syndrome. It stratifies long-term risk, with a higher score meaning higher risk.

set1.q: Which electrocardiogram finding persists for months after an ST-elevation infarction?
opts: ST elevation
ST elevation appears in the first minutes to hours and settles back over about a week. The Q wave is what persists for months.
Reciprocal ST depression
Reciprocal depression on the opposite side accompanies acute ST elevation and supports the diagnosis. The finding that persists for months is the Q wave.
The Q wave
Correct. The infarct evolves from hyperacute T waves and ST elevation (minutes to hours) to T inversion with a Q wave (hours to a day), a coronary T at a week, and a Q wave that persists for months.
Hyperacute T waves
Hyperacute T waves are the earliest change, in the first minutes to hours. The finding that persists for months is the Q wave, meaning the infarct has already happened.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set1.q: Microvascular angina is more frequent in which group?
opts: Men
Male sex is a nonmodifiable risk factor for atherosclerotic coronary artery disease. Microvascular angina is more frequent in females, often with stress or anxiety.
Children
No pediatric pattern is described. Microvascular angina is more frequent in adult females and is often associated with stress or anxiety.
Smokers
Smoking is the major risk factor for vasospastic angina. Microvascular angina is more frequent in females, often associated with stress or anxiety.
Women
Correct. Microvascular angina is more frequent in females and is often associated with stress or anxiety; estrogen deficiency is among its proposed mechanisms.

set1.q: Why does angina typically worsen with exertion?
opts: Exertion lowers heart rate
Exertion raises the heart rate, not lowers it. It raises myocardial oxygen demand beyond what a narrowed artery can supply.
Exertion dissolves the plaque
Exertion does not dissolve plaque. It raises oxygen demand, and the fixed narrowing cannot increase supply to meet it.
Exertion blocks the coronary valve
There is no coronary valve to block. Angina worsens with exertion because oxygen demand rises past what the narrowed artery supplies.
Exertion raises oxygen demand
Correct. Exercise and emotional stress raise myocardial oxygen demand; a narrowed artery cannot raise supply to match, so the supply and demand mismatch produces pain.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set1.q: What is the 99th-percentile high-sensitivity troponin I value for men, in ng/L?
opts: Two ng/L is at the low end of high-sensitivity troponin I measurement, not a cut-off. The men's 99th percentile is 20 ng/L.
Correct. The high-sensitivity troponin I 99th percentile is 20 ng/L for men and 12 ng/L for women; values above them are abnormal. These sex-specific numbers are ones to know.
Twelve ng/L is the women's high-sensitivity troponin I 99th percentile. The men's value is higher, at 20.
Thirty sits above both sex-specific values. High-sensitivity troponin I is abnormal above 20 ng/L in men.
set1.cite: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

set1.q: After initial stabilization of unstable angina, which procedure follows?
opts: Thrombolytic therapy
Thrombolytics are for ST-elevation infarction when intervention is 2 or more hours away. After stabilization of unstable angina, left heart catheterization follows.
Left heart catheterization

Correct. Following initial stabilization, left heart catheterization introduces a guidewire to the coronary arteries, allowing coronary angiography to find the lesion and angioplasty or stenting to open it.
Discharge and follow-up
Unstable angina is an acute coronary syndrome and a medical emergency, not a discharge. After stabilization the next step is left heart catheterization.
Repeat stress test
Stress testing belongs to the stable workup. After stabilization of an acute coronary syndrome, left heart catheterization with angiography follows.

set1.q: Which stress-test electrocardiogram change is usual in stable angina?
opts: Bundle branch block
A new left bundle branch block is treated as an ST-elevation equivalent in suspected infarction. The usual stress-induced change in stable angina is T-wave inversion.
T-wave inversion
Correct. Stable angina is diagnosed by stress-test-induced electrocardiogram changes, usually T-wave inversion, on an exercise treadmill test, a nuclear stress test or cardiac computed tomography.
ST elevation
ST elevation over 1 mm in two or more consecutive leads is the ST-elevation myocardial infarction pattern. The usual stress-induced change in stable angina is T-wave inversion.
New Q waves
Pathologic Q waves mean an infarction has already happened; they are not a stress-induced ischemic change. Stable angina usually shows T-wave inversion under stress.

set1.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
set1.q: When is a beta blocker withheld in ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: When there is hypertension
Hypertension is not a reason to withhold a beta blocker. It is given unless the patient is bradycardic.
When there is tachycardia
A fast heart rate is not the contraindication; slowing the rate lowers oxygen demand. The beta blocker is withheld for bradycardia.
When pain persists
Ongoing pain is not a reason to withhold it. The beta blocker is given in ST-elevation infarction unless there is bradycardia.
When there is bradycardia
Correct. ST-elevation infarction treatment includes a beta blocker if there is no bradycardia, along with nitroglycerin, aspirin and a call to the catheterization team.

set1.q: Which term describes passing a guidewire into the heart chambers and coronary arteries?
opts: Left heart catheterization

Correct. Left heart catheterization is the introduction of a guidewire and access to the chambers of the heart and the coronary arteries. The terms are not interchangeable: the catheter is the access.
Coronary angiography
Coronary angiography is the dye study done once access is gained: contrast is injected to identify the lesion. The guidewire access itself is the left heart catheterization.
Coronary angioplasty
Coronary angioplasty uses a device to balloon open a narrowed artery. It follows access and angiography; the guidewire access itself is called left heart catheterization.
Coronary artery bypass
Coronary artery bypass grafting is open surgery that sews an artery or vein beyond the blockage. Passing a guidewire into the heart is left heart catheterization.

set1.q: What is troponin best used for in chest pain?
opts: Locating the culprit artery
Troponin cannot say which artery is blocked; lead groups and angiography do that. Troponin is used to rule infarction out.
Replacing the electrocardiogram
Every chest pain patient still gets a stat electrocardiogram. Troponin adds a rule-out tool, not a replacement.
Ruling infarction out
Correct. High-sensitivity troponin identifies who can safely go home: it is a rule-out tool rather than a positive predictor of who is definitely having a heart attack.
Ruling infarction in
Troponin is less a positive predictor than a rule-out tool. Its strength is showing who can safely be sent home.
set1.cite: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

set1.q: Subendocardial ischemia produces which change in the overlying leads?
opts: Hyperacute T waves
Hyperacute T waves are the earliest stage of an evolving ST-elevation infarction. Subendocardial ischemia produces ST depression over the ischemic region.
ST depression
Correct. Subendocardial ischemia, limited to the inner wall, gives ST depression in the leads overlying the region; transmural ischemia through the full wall thickness gives ST elevation.
ST elevation
ST elevation over the region comes from transmural ischemia through the full thickness of the wall. Subendocardial ischemia produces ST depression.
Pathologic Q waves
Pathologic Q waves appear after an infarct has already happened and persist for months. Subendocardial ischemia produces ST depression.

set1.q: What gesture is Levine's sign?
opts: A finger pointing to one spot
Pointing with one finger to a single spot is the pointing sign. Levine's sign is a clenched fist over the sternum.
A hand gripping the left arm
Gripping the opposite arm is the arm sign. Levine's sign is a clenched fist held over the sternum.
A clenched fist over the sternum
Correct. Levine's sign is the patient holding a clenched fist over the sternum to describe the chest discomfort, a classic gesture of ischemic chest pain.
An open palm flat on the chest
An open palm flat on the chest is the palm sign. Levine's sign is a clenched fist held over the sternum.

set1.q: Which drug can precipitate vasospastic angina?
opts: Cocaine
Correct. Drugs that may precipitate vasospastic angina are cocaine, ephedrine, marijuana, alcohol, amphetamine and triptans. Triptans are also on the list of drugs to avoid in the condition.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, the first-line therapy for vasospastic angina, so it prevents rather than precipitates spasm. Cocaine is a precipitant.
Amlodipine
Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker used first-line in vasospastic angina. The precipitating drugs include cocaine, ephedrine, marijuana, alcohol, amphetamine and triptans.
Nitroglycerin
Vasospastic angina responds to nitroglycerin, and nitrates are its symptomatic treatment. Cocaine, amphetamine and triptans are among the drugs that precipitate it.

set1.q: Which electrocardiogram pattern marks a right ventricular infarct?
opts: ST depression in V1 to V3
ST depression in V1 to V3 is the reciprocal picture of a posterior infarct, confirmed with V7 to V9. A right ventricular infarct shows ST elevation in V1 and V4R.
ST elevation in V5 and V6
ST elevation in V5 and V6 is lateral, pointing to the circumflex. A right ventricular infarct shows ST elevation in V1 and the right-sided lead V4R.
ST elevation in I and aVL
I and aVL are the leads that show reciprocal ST depression in a right ventricular infarct. The elevation itself is in V1 and V4R.
ST elevation in V1 and V4R
Correct. A right ventricular infarct shows ST elevation in V1 and the right-sided lead V4R, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL; the culprit is the right coronary artery.

set1.q: What separates unstable angina from non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: Response to nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin usually helps unstable angina and may help infarction pain, so the response does not separate them. An elevated troponin marks the infarction.
The troponin level
Correct. Elevated troponin or high-sensitivity troponin is what differentiates non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction from unstable angina, in which troponin is normal. Both can occur at rest.
Pain at rest
Pain at rest occurs in both: it defines unstable angina and is common in infarction. The discriminator is the troponin level, normal in unstable angina and elevated in infarction.
Where the pain radiates
Referral to the jaw, arm or back occurs across acute coronary syndromes and does not separate them. The troponin level is the discriminator.

set1.q: Which muscle type contains no troponin?
opts: Skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle contains troponins alongside cardiac muscle. Smooth muscle cells contain none.
Diaphragm muscle
The diaphragm is skeletal muscle, which contains troponins. Only smooth muscle lacks them.
Smooth muscle
Correct. Troponins are protein molecules of cardiac and skeletal muscle; smooth muscle cells do not contain troponins. Of the three types, troponin I is specific to the heart.
Cardiac muscle
Cardiac muscle contains troponin, including the heart-specific troponin I. The muscle type without troponin is smooth muscle.
set1.cite: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

set1.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
set1.q: Which thrombolytic is most commonly used today?
opts: Streptokinase
Streptokinase is an older fibrinolytic still on the list, but not the most used. Tenecteplase is the most common today.
Anistreplase
Anistreplase is on the fibrinolytic list but is not the most used agent. Tenecteplase is the most common today.
Lanoteplase
Lanoteplase is on the fibrinolytic list but is not the agent of choice. Tenecteplase is the most common fibrinolytic today.
Tenecteplase
Correct. Tenecteplase is the most common fibrinolytic today. Others include alteplase (tissue plasminogen activator), reteplase, streptokinase, anistreplase and lanoteplase.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following coronary artery disease:
set1.q: Which components make up an atherosclerotic plaque?
opts: Fat, smooth muscle and fibroblasts
Correct. Atherosclerosis is built of fat, smooth muscle, fibroblasts and intracellular matrix components, with macrophages turned foam cells beneath a fibrous cap.
Fibrin, platelets and red cells
Fibrin, platelets and red cells make a thrombus, which forms after a plaque ruptures. The plaque itself is fat, smooth muscle, fibroblasts and matrix.
Elastin, cartilage and bone
Cartilage and bone are not plaque components. An atherosclerotic plaque is fat, smooth muscle, fibroblasts and intracellular matrix.
Neutrophils, pus and bacteria
That describes an abscess, an infection. An atherosclerotic plaque is fat, smooth muscle, fibroblasts and intracellular matrix components.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set1.q: What is the 99th-percentile high-sensitivity troponin I value for women, in ng/L?
opts: Thirty is above both sex-specific values. The high-sensitivity troponin I 99th percentile is 12 ng/L in women and 20 ng/L in men.
Two ng/L is near the bottom of what the high-sensitivity troponin I assay measures, not the women's cut-off, which is 12 ng/L.
Correct. High-sensitivity troponin I has sex-specific 99th percentiles: 12 ng/L for women and 20 ng/L for men. A woman above 12 ng/L of troponin I is abnormal.
Twenty ng/L is the men's 99th percentile for high-sensitivity troponin I. The women's value is lower, at 12.
set1.cite: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

set1.q: When should a patient using nitroglycerin for angina call emergency medical services?
opts: Pain that starts with exercise
Pain brought on by exertion and relieved by rest is the stable pattern itself. The call comes when pain is unimproved five minutes after one nitroglycerin dose.
Pain unimproved 5 minutes after one dose
Correct. Emergency medical services are called if the chest pain is unimproved or worsening five minutes after one nitroglycerin dose, or if three consecutive doses have failed to relieve it.
Pain that needs any dose at all
Needing a dose is ordinary stable angina care: nitroglycerin is the cornerstone of therapy. The call comes when pain is unimproved five minutes after one dose.
Only after five doses have failed
Waiting for five doses is too long. The rule is to call if pain is unimproved five minutes after one dose, or if three consecutive doses have failed.

set2.q: Which statement defines angina pectoris?
opts: Permanent scarring of the ventricle
Permanent scarring follows infarction. Angina pectoris is transient ischemia, not long or severe enough to kill muscle.
Inflammation of the pericardium
Pericardial inflammation is pericarditis. Angina pectoris is transient, recurrent myocardial ischemia short of infarction.
Transient ischemia short of infarction
Correct. Angina pectoris is transient myocardial ischemia that is not long or severe enough to cause infarction, and its symptoms are recurrent.
Myocardial necrosis with ST elevation
Necrosis with ST elevation is an ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Angina is transient ischemia that stops short of infarction.

set2.q: How is non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated compared with unstable angina?
opts: Observation only
Both are acute coronary syndromes and a medical emergency, so observation alone is not enough. A non-ST-elevation infarction is treated the same as unstable angina.
The same way

Correct. A non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction is treated the same as unstable angina: a medical emergency with chewable aspirin, a beta blocker, intravenous nitrates and antithrombotic therapy, then catheterization.
As an ST-elevation infarct
The ST-elevation pathway (catheterization team at once, door-to-balloon under 90 minutes) is for ST elevation. A non-ST-elevation infarction is treated the same as unstable angina.
Thrombolytics first
Thrombolytics belong to ST-elevation infarction when intervention is 2 or more hours away. A non-ST-elevation infarction is treated the same as unstable angina.

set2.q: Which coronary artery supplies the atrioventricular node?
opts: Left marginal artery
The left marginal artery supplies the left ventricle's lateral wall. The atrioventricular node takes its supply from the right coronary artery.
Right coronary artery
Correct. The right coronary artery supplies the atrioventricular node, which is why right coronary artery occlusion is the one most likely to lead to dysrhythmias such as complete heart block.
Left anterior descending artery
The left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) artery supplies the anterior wall and most of the septum. The atrioventricular node is supplied by the right coronary artery.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the lateral wall and gives the sinoatrial node branch in about 40% of people. The atrioventricular node is supplied by the right coronary artery.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set2.q: From what age is age itself a coronary risk factor in men?
opts: 65 years
Sixty-five is too late. Age counts as a nonmodifiable risk factor from 45 years in men and 55 in women.
35 years
Thirty-five is too early. Age becomes a coronary risk factor at 45 years in men and 55 years in women.
45 years
Correct. Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor from 45 years in men and from 55 years in women; men carry more risk than premenopausal women, a gap that narrows with age.
55 years
Fifty-five is the threshold for women. For men, age becomes a nonmodifiable coronary risk factor at 45 years.

set2.q: Above which standard troponin I value, in ng/mL, is the result abnormal?
opts: That is ten times too low; nearly everyone would read abnormal. The standard troponin I abnormal value is above 0.04 ng/mL.
Correct. The 99th percentile for the standard troponin I assay is 0.04 ng/mL; a standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal, and a result at or below it is reported as not abnormal.
A threshold of 0.4 is ten times too high and would miss injury. Standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal.
Four is a hundred times the cut-off. A standard troponin I result is abnormal above 0.04 ng/mL, its 99th percentile.
set2.cite: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

set2.q: ST elevation in V1 through V4 points to which culprit artery?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery is the culprit for inferior changes in II, III and aVF. Anterior and septal changes in V1 through V4 point to the left anterior descending artery.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex is the culprit for lateral changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6. V1 through V4 point to the left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) artery.
Right marginal branch
The right marginal branch comes off the right coronary artery and supplies the right ventricle. V1 through V4 point to the left anterior descending artery.
Left anterior descending
Correct. The anterior and septal leads V1 through V4 point to the left anterior descending artery, now named the anterior interventricular artery, the most common culprit in acute infarction.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set2.q: How does the coronary risk gap between men and women change with age?
opts: It narrows by about 80
Correct. Men carry more risk than premenopausal women, but the difference narrows with age and is close to even by about 80.
It widens every decade
The gap does not widen. Men carry more risk than premenopausal women, and the difference narrows until it is about even by 80.
It stays fixed for life
It is not fixed. The male excess over premenopausal women narrows with age and has nearly closed by about 80.
It favors women at 40
At 40 men carry more risk than premenopausal women. The gap between the sexes narrows with age, closing by about 80.

set2.q: Which feature marks angina as unstable rather than stable?
opts: Pain at rest
Correct. Stable angina is relieved by rest; unstable angina occurs at rest. Pain at rest, new-onset angina that limits activity, or angina that is increasing makes the pattern unstable.
Pain with exertion
Pain brought on by exertion is the stable pattern: activity raises oxygen demand and rest relieves it. Unstable angina is marked by pain at rest.
Relief with nitroglycerin
Stable angina is relieved by nitroglycerin, and unstable angina usually is too, so relief does not separate them. Pain occurring at rest marks the unstable pattern.
Substernal pressure
Substernal chest pressure is the typical description of ischemic pain in any angina. It is pain at rest that marks the angina as unstable.

set2.q: On a standard 12-lead electrocardiogram, how does a posterior infarct appear?
opts: ST depression in V1 to V3
Correct. A posterior infarct shows as ST depression in V1 to V3, the reciprocal of ST elevation on the back of the heart. It is easy to miss, and posterior leads V7 to V9 confirm it.
ST elevation in V1 to V3
ST elevation in the anterior and septal leads points to the left anterior descending artery. A posterior infarct shows as ST depression in V1 to V3.
ST elevation in II, III, aVF
ST elevation in II, III and aVF is an inferior infarct from the right coronary artery. A posterior infarct shows as ST depression in V1 to V3.
ST depression in V5 and V6
V5 and V6 are lateral leads, not the mirror of the back wall. A posterior infarct shows as ST depression in V1 to V3.

set2.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
set2.q: In roughly what share of right coronary occlusions does the infarct extend into the right ventricle?
opts: Correct. Right coronary occlusion affects the inferior and posterior left ventricular wall and the septum, and extends into the right ventricle in 15% to 30% of cases.
Right ventricular extension is not that rare. It occurs in 15% to 30% of right coronary occlusions, which is why the right ventricle is looked for.
Most right coronary occlusions spare the right ventricle. Extension into the right ventricle occurs in 15% to 30% of cases.
Over 90%
Right ventricular involvement is the minority, not the rule. It occurs in 15% to 30% of right coronary occlusions.

set2.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
set2.q: When is a thrombolytic given for ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: When chest pain has resolved
Pain relief does not trigger lytics. Thrombolytics are given when the nearest percutaneous intervention unit is 2 or more hours away.
When intervention is 2+ hours away
Correct. If the closest percutaneous coronary intervention unit is 2 or more hours away, thrombolytics are given, started within 30 minutes of arrival. They carry a risk of intracerebral hemorrhage.
When troponin is still normal
Troponin does not decide lytic therapy; ST elevation does. Thrombolytics are given when the nearest intervention unit is 2 or more hours away.
For every patient on arrival
Thrombolytics are not routine because they risk intracerebral hemorrhage. They are given when the nearest intervention unit is 2 or more hours away.

set2.q: Which agent is delivered at angiography to provoke coronary spasm?
opts: Nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin is what relieves the provoked spasm through the catheter, and vasospasm responds to it. The provoking agent is ergonovine or acetylcholine.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, first-line to prevent vasospasm, so it would blunt rather than provoke spasm. Ergonovine or acetylcholine provokes it.
Amlodipine
Amlodipine is a first-line calcium channel blocker for vasospastic angina, used to prevent spasm. The agent given to provoke it at angiography is ergonovine or acetylcholine.
Ergonovine
Correct. Ergonovine or acetylcholine is delivered during angiography; coronary spasm that then resolves with nitroglycerin through the catheter is the gold standard for vasospastic angina.

set2.q: When is a stent usually placed during percutaneous coronary intervention?
opts: Only after a failed atherectomy
Atherectomy is an option during the intervention, not a gate the stent must wait for. The stent is usually placed after balloon pre-dilation, and direct stenting may do better.
Only after bypass grafting
Bypass grafting is open surgery, an alternative to a stent rather than a step before one. During the intervention the stent usually follows balloon pre-dilation.
After balloon pre-dilation
Correct. The stent is usually placed after balloon pre-dilation of the narrowed segment. Direct stenting, without pre-dilation, may lead to better outcomes, so the order is not absolute.
Before any guidewire is passed
Nothing can be placed before access: the guidewire of the catheterization comes first. The stent then usually follows balloon pre-dilation of the narrowed segment.

set2.q: How does body position affect the pain of angina pectoris?
opts: Leaning forward relieves it
Angina pain is not positional, so leaning forward does not change it. Exertion worsens it; rest and nitroglycerin relieve it.
Sitting upright worsens it
Position does not alter angina. What worsens the pain is exertion, which raises myocardial oxygen demand.
It does not change it
Correct. The pain of angina pectoris is not affected by position; it typically worsens with exertion. Pain that changes with position lowers the suspicion that it is cardiac.
Lying flat relieves it
Lying flat does not relieve angina, because angina pain is not affected by position. Rest and nitroglycerin relieve it.

set2.q: When a vein is used for coronary bypass, what does it connect?
opts: The two ends of the blocked segment only
A vein graft does not simply bridge the plaque from end to end. It forms a connection between the aorta and the coronary artery beyond the obstruction.
The aorta and the coronary beyond the block
Correct. A vein graft, usually the great saphenous vein, forms a connection between the aorta and the coronary artery distal to the obstruction. It is used when an artery cannot be.
The coronary artery and the coronary sinus
Joining a coronary artery to the coronary sinus would send blood straight into the venous return. A vein graft runs from the aorta to the coronary artery distal to the obstruction.
The pulmonary artery and the coronary artery
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and is never a graft source. A vein graft carries aortic blood to the coronary artery distal to the obstruction.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following coronary artery disease:
set2.q: What is true of coronary artery distribution from person to person?
opts: It differs only between sexes
Sex is not what sorts it. Distribution varies individually, for example which artery gives the posterior interventricular branch and supplies the sinoatrial node.
It is fixed by the left main
No single vessel fixes the pattern. Anatomical variation in distribution is common, which is why the culprit artery is predicted, not known, from the leads.
It varies between people
Correct. Coronary distribution varies: which artery gives the posterior interventricular branch, and which supplies the sinoatrial node, differs between people, so the culprit artery is a best guess.
It is identical in everyone
It is not identical: the sinoatrial node, for example, is supplied by the right coronary artery in about 60% and by the circumflex in about 40%.

set2.q: Missing dual antiplatelet doses in the first 6 weeks after a stent carries what risk of sudden in-stent restenosis?
opts: About 5%
The risk is far higher than one in twenty. Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy in the first 6 weeks gives about a 50% risk of sudden in-stent restenosis, which is why adherence is stressed.
About 20%
One in five understates it. Noncompliance in the first 6 weeks carries about a 50% risk of sudden in-stent restenosis, the coin flip that makes adherence the key teaching point.
Close to 100%
Restenosis is not certain. Noncompliance in the first 6 weeks gives about a 50% risk, a coin flip, which is still high enough that taking every dose is the central instruction.
About 50%
Correct. Noncompliance with dual antiplatelet therapy in the first 6 weeks carries a 50% risk of sudden in-stent restenosis, a coin flip. Patients are taught that they have to take these medications.

set2.q: When is oxygen given in unstable angina or non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: To every patient on arrival
Routine oxygen for everyone is the old MONA (morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin) habit. Oxygen is given only if the oxygen saturation is below 91%.
Only while pain continues
Ongoing pain is not the trigger for oxygen. It is given only if the oxygen saturation is below 91%; with normal oxygenation it causes peripheral vasoconstriction.
Only after catheterization
Catheterization timing does not decide oxygen use. Oxygen is given at any point only if the oxygen saturation is below 91%, and withheld when it is normal.
Only if SpO2 is under 91%

Correct. MONA (morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin) is outdated: oxygen is given only if the oxygen saturation is below 91%. With normal oxygenation it is not given, because it causes peripheral vasoconstriction.

set2.q: What separates non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction from unstable angina?
opts: Relief with nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin usually helps unstable angina and may help the infarction's pain. The separator is an elevated troponin.
An elevated troponin
Correct. Elevated troponin (standard or high-sensitivity) is what differentiates non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction from unstable angina, whose troponin levels are normal.
Pain at rest
Pain at rest occurs in both; it is part of unstable angina's definition. The separator is an elevated troponin in the infarction.
T-wave inversion
T-wave changes can appear in both. What separates the infarction from unstable angina is an elevated troponin.

set2.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
set2.q: Which drug is avoided in a right ventricular infarct?
opts: Nitroglycerin

Correct. In a right ventricular infarct nitroglycerin is not given: lowering preload removes the Frank-Starling support the failing right ventricle depends on, dropping output and precipitating shock.
Aspirin
Chewable aspirin is given in every ST-elevation infarction, right ventricular or not. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.
Heparin
A heparin drip is given once catheterization is confirmed, whatever the territory. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is a P2Y12 antagonist given once catheterization is confirmed. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.

set2.q: Which is the most common form of angina pectoris?
opts: Vasospastic angina
Vasospastic angina is relatively uncommon: spasm of a coronary artery, often under age 50, at rest and early in the morning. Stable angina is the most common form.
Microvascular angina
Microvascular angina is angina with normal coronary arteries on angiography, a diagnosis of exclusion seen more often in women. Stable angina is the most common form.
Stable angina
Correct. Stable angina, also called stable ischemic heart disease, is the most common form of angina pectoris. It is usually brought on by activity and relieved by rest and nitroglycerin.
Unstable angina
Unstable angina is a change in a stable pattern (pain at rest, new limiting pain or worsening pain) and is an acute coronary syndrome. The most common form is stable angina.

set2.q: Microvascular angina was formerly called what?
opts: Stable ischemic disease
Stable ischemic heart disease is the other name for stable angina, the most common form. Microvascular angina was formerly called cardiac syndrome X.
Cardiac syndrome X
Correct. Microvascular angina was formerly called cardiac syndrome X: angina with ST changes, possibly elevated biomarkers, but normal coronary arteries on angiography.
Prinzmetal angina
Prinzmetal angina is another name for vasospastic, or variant, angina: coronary spasm at rest. Microvascular angina was formerly called cardiac syndrome X.
Dressler syndrome
Dressler syndrome is pericarditis after a myocardial infarction. The former name of microvascular angina is cardiac syndrome X.

set2.q: Which word appears among the recognized angina descriptors?
opts: Toothache
Correct. Angina may be described as squeezing, tightness, pressure, constriction, burning, heartburn, fullness, band-like, or even a toothache, so an odd word does not exclude it.
Stabbing
Stabbing is not among the angina descriptors, which are squeezing, tightness, pressure, constriction, burning, heartburn, fullness, band-like and toothache.
Pleuritic
Pain that changes with breathing is not an angina descriptor. The descriptors are pressure-type words such as squeezing, tightness, band-like, even toothache.
Shooting
Shooting is not on the descriptor list. Angina is squeezing, tightness, pressure, constriction, burning, heartburn, fullness, band-like or toothache.

set2.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
set2.q: What does the T in the HEART score stand for?
opts: Troponin
Correct. HEART (History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, Troponin) scores the initial troponin as its last component; the score is one of several acute coronary syndrome risk scores.
Timing of pain
Timing is not a HEART component. The five are History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors and Troponin, the initial troponin level.
Treadmill result
No stress test is part of the score. HEART (History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, Troponin) uses the initial troponin.
Temperature
Temperature plays no part. The HEART score's letters are History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors and Troponin.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set2.q: Vasospastic angina most often affects which age group?
opts: Mainly infants
No pediatric pattern is described for vasospasm. Vasospastic angina is an adult condition, often in patients under 50, with smoking as a major risk factor.
Mostly over 80
By 80 the sex gap in atherosclerotic risk has narrowed, but that is not vasospasm. Vasospastic angina is often seen in patients under 50.
Often under 50
Correct. Vasospastic angina is relatively uncommon and often affects people under 50, younger than the typical patient with atherosclerotic coronary artery disease.
Often over 70
An older group is the typical atherosclerotic picture, with risk starting at 45 in men and 55 in women. Vasospastic angina is often seen under 50.

set2.q: Once myocardial ischemia begins, within what time does irreversible injury occur?
opts: 5 to 10 minutes
Five to ten minutes is too short. Ischemia becomes irreversible injury at about 40 to 60 minutes, the window that drives rapid reperfusion.
6 to 12 hours
Waiting hours would forfeit the muscle. Irreversible injury occurs in about 40 to 60 minutes of ischemia, so reperfusion is a race against the clock.
2 to 3 days
Days is far too long. Myocardial injury becomes irreversible at about 40 to 60 minutes, which is why every step of infarction care is timed.
40 to 60 minutes
Correct. Irreversible myocardial injury occurs in about 40 to 60 minutes of ischemia, which is why the treatment of an acute infarction is built around time: time is muscle.

set2.q: What does coronary angiography show in microvascular angina?
opts: Left main narrowing
Left main narrowing is obstructive atherosclerotic disease. Microvascular angina is defined by normal coronary arteries on angiography.
Normal coronary arteries
Correct. Microvascular angina is angina with ST changes, possibly even elevated cardiac biomarkers, but normal coronary arteries on the angiogram.
A single occluded vessel
An occluded epicardial artery is atherosclerotic coronary artery disease. In microvascular angina, the angiogram shows normal coronary arteries.
Provoked coronary spasm
Spasm provoked by ergonovine or acetylcholine is the gold standard for vasospastic angina. In microvascular angina the coronary arteries look normal.

set2.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
set2.q: What is the goal door-to-balloon time for ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: Under 10 minutes
Ten minutes is the target for obtaining the electrocardiogram after arrival. The door-to-balloon goal is under 90 minutes.
Under 30 minutes
Thirty minutes is the window for starting thrombolytics when intervention is far away. The door-to-balloon goal is under 90 minutes.
Under 4 hours
Four hours is far too long for an occluded artery; time is muscle. The door-to-balloon goal is under 90 minutes.
Under 90 minutes
Correct. Time is muscle: the goal door-to-balloon time is under 90 minutes, after an electrocardiogram within 10 minutes of arrival.

set2.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
set2.q: Cardiogenic shock after infarction is more common with which infarcts?
opts: Right-sided infarcts
Right-sided infarcts can tip into shock if preload is dropped, for example with nitroglycerin, but cardiogenic shock as a complication is more common in left-sided infarcts.
Silent infarcts
Silent ischemia describes absent chest discomfort, as in diabetes or neuropathy; it says nothing about shock risk. Cardiogenic shock is more common in left-sided infarcts.
Vasospastic episodes
Vasospastic episodes are transient and resolve, usually within 5 to 15 minutes, in arteries without high-grade stenosis. Cardiogenic shock is more common after left-sided infarcts.
Left-sided infarcts

Correct. Cardiogenic shock is a mechanical complication of myocardial infarction that is more common in left-sided infarcts, in keeping with left ventricular involvement carrying the higher mortality.

set2.q: How does the pain of unstable angina respond to nitroglycerin?
opts: Usually relieved, not always
Correct. In unstable angina, nitroglycerin usually (but not always) helps. Stable angina is reliably relieved by rest and nitroglycerin, and infarction pain may or may not respond.
Always completely relieved
Reliable relief with rest and nitroglycerin is the stable pattern. In unstable angina nitroglycerin usually, but not always, helps.
Never relieved at all
Unstable angina is not nitroglycerin-resistant as a rule: it usually helps, though not always. Failure to respond is not what defines it.
Made worse by the drug
Nitroglycerin does not worsen unstable angina pain; it usually helps, though not always. It is withheld in a right ventricular infarct, not in angina.
